To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the US is not a high energy consuming country, and that Japan is not a low energy consuming country.
Japan is 3.6 times more efficient than the US in terms of energy intensity, but only 2.2 times in terms of TPER/GDP.
Japan is 3.5 times more efficient than the US in energy use, and that the US consumes about 23% more primary energy than Japan.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following points: (1) the definition of energy intensity, (2) the estimation of a single indicator for international comparison, (3) a comparison of the US and Japan.
the following three issues: (i) the definition of energy intensity; (ii) the definition of GDP; and (iii) the relationship between energy intensity and GDP.
how we can measure the real gap of energy intensity between the US and other countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, although the US is less energy-efficient than Japan in the use of energy, the US is not as inefficient as is generally thought.
the US consumes about 1.5 times more energy than Japan.
the US consumes more energy than Japan.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the US consumes about three times more energy than Japan per dollar of GDP.
Japan is more efficient than the US, but the gap is not so large.
the US consumes more than twice as much energy as Japan, but the US economy is 3.4 times larger than that of Japan.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single, real and comparable measure of energy efficiency should be developed and used for international comparison.
TPER/GDP is an inappropriate measure for international comparisons of energy intensity.
a more accurate energy intensity indicator is required to assess national efficiency and to compare energy efficiency among countries.
